Question: What are some possible reasons for pilots having trouble with landings? Is it a difficult task for pilots, or could nerves play a role?
Answer: Yes, it’s difficult. The margin for error is small. The aircraft is flying right at the stall margin, the winds are often unpredictable and seldom aligned with the runway heading. You have to control three variables simultaneously - lineup, rate of descent, and aircraft AoA (or airspeed). The effect of power changes at landing speeds are more pronounced. And once on the runway, you still have to control the aircraft to affect a safe stop, occasionally on a wet or icy runway, and often with crosswinds. And sometimes, even the runway is moving.

Question: Are information about military equipment capabilities like fighter jets of different countries all publicly available on the internet? If so, why don't countries take advantage of these and build their own military equipment?
Answer: Some basic information (weight, ceiling, max speed, etc.) are publicly available on the internet and in other publications such as Jane’s Ships. And countries do take advantage of this information. But every military fighter has classified information regarding weapons deployment, systems capabilities, performance tables, EW suites, RCS, etc. that is definitely not publicly available on the internet. Additionally, just because I you can find the dimensions, weight, and thrust (and so on) of an aircraft in no way provides the information to build that aircraft. Not even close. Manufacturing techniques and materials are not publicly disclosed, and certain materials, such as stealth coatings, are definitely classified. For example, there is no publicly available information that can tell you how to build the vertical control systems for this AV-8B Harrier II. It is amazingly complex and sophisticated. Here — try this. Tell me what the shape, material, design, and purpose is for those semi-circular horizontal plates located just above the engine intake. What are those for, and how do you build them to meet that purpose. It’s simply not possible to do that from the publicly available information. It is way too limited. Not to mention the sheer investment required to build and test military aircraft. Just the cost of a wind tunnel alone is enough to drain your wallet, let alone the other test gear required. It’s an enormous expense that very few countries can afford. So there’s that…

Question: Can you describe your most impressive, speedup of programming code you did in a project that was already essentially done?
Answer: In the early 90s, I was working for an IT consulting company that was building a new, custom client-server app to manage ship overhauls for the US Navy. We built the application and fielded it. It was quite successful and a well designed product. We implemented the product at six Navy Shipyards. It was way better than what they had been using. Yeah team! However, we DID NOT perform sufficient performance testing before releasing the product, and it showed soon after it was in the field. The problem was mainly that Oracle database, which despite having an Oracle engineer working alongside us, was simply not optimized. And neither were the client-side queries. And neither were the Sun servers. I led a SWAT team to specifically address performance issues. We worked for weeks tuning every query, analyzing every database index, examining every business process, and tweeking the hardware (Sun servers - we also had Sun engineers help us). We focused our efforts on the parts of the application that were used most frequently; where the performance improvements would have high visibility. It took a real effort, but it was successful. We increase performance in the most critical areas by 50%, easily. And in a few areas as much as 90%. And boy did we learn a lot about performance tuning, SQL queries, and hardware settings. I ran more Oracle query traces than I can count. And given the nature of the contract with the Navy, we had to conduct all of this performance-tuning on our own dime, which was hard for a for-profit company. But having the multi-million dollar project fail due to performance issues was simply not an option. Oh…and never, ever again did we release a product without conducting serious, significant performance testing.

Question: How did aviation go from the Wright Brothers' first flight to the B-52 Stratofortress in just over 48 years? Is that the most rapid and remarkable technical advance in human history?

And that’s not to mention that we’ve walked on the Moon and landed a rover on Mars. I’m stunned. There are, of course, a lot of similar technological advances. Digital computers were invented (more or less) during WWII. The ENIAC arrived in 1945. And it took a long time to move from those early devices to the PC…~36 years. And then…seemingly overnight…we’re all walking around with the power of an IBM 360 in our hip pocket. That took only 24 years and boy look how that has changed our world. Rocket technology showed a similar leap. But I do agree with you…the progress in aviation has just accelerated remarkably fast. Wilbur and Orville would be proud.

Question: Why does the USAF get mad when the US Army gets fixed wing craft but the USN doesn't get mad when the US Army has their own transport ships?
Answer: History, tradition, the constant battle over “roles & missions”. Competition for the biggest share of the DoD budget. it’s a long, long story. I worked for the Secretary of Defense for 3 years. At the most senior levels of the military Services, there is a constant battle ongoing for money…the DoD Budget. It’s typically viewed as a zero-sum game; if the Army gets more $s for tanks, it means the USAF gets less $s for bombers. And that battle has been going on since the USAF became a separate Service in 1947. Before that, as you may recall, it was the Army Air Corps…and the US Army hasn’t forgotten that. So between the USA and USAF, there is an ongoing battle over who can operate fixed-wing aircraft. The USAF has surrendered operation of helicopters to the USA and USMC, but fixed-wing aircraft are still the USAF’s “rice bowl” and they defend that with passion. The Navy is a bit different. The USN is divided into three main groups: Aviation, Surface, and Submarine. The epitome of Aviation is of course an aircraft carrier. For Surface it’s a guided missile cruiser, and for Submarine there’s the newest attack boat, the Virginia class. (Note: There is the “gator Navy” that supports amphibious landings and works closely with the USMC. It’s kind of a combination between Surface and Aviation though.) The point is that the USN roles don’t really compete with the US Army ships, which are mostly landing craft and logistics support vessels. The USA operate less than 100 vessels, so no big whoop; have at it. The USN does compete with the USAF for aircraft and missiles: F-16s versus carrier-based F/A-18s, and for ballistic missiles; ground-based versus sea-based ICBMs.

Question: Was the F-117 Nighthawk difficult to fly? Why was this stealth fighter jet retired from service?
Answer: I was told “yes”, it is difficult to fly. Inherently unstable and only computerized fly-by-wire allows for control. The “V” tail provided very limited nose pitch authority; nothing like a normal horizontal stabilizer. The story is that one F-117 that was lost in the mid-80s was because a pilot flying a circuit round-robin late at night (because they could only fly at night due to secrecy)…he was bored to tears and decided to try a barrel roll. In a normal fighter aircraft, this is no big deal. In fact part of the confidence training is actually doing aerobatics at night, completely on the gauges. He got the nose a bit too far down, and the tail simply did not have the aerodynamic force to pull the nose back up. It’s possible the pilot was severely disoriented. Pilot was lost. Scratch one Nighthawk. It was retired because better solutions were available; stealth technology improved considerably. The F-117 was a first Very Low Observable (VLO) aircraft. It worked, but the ability to develop the complex curves necessary for stealth simply did not exist back in the late 70s/early 80s; so they relied on a faceted design. It was a point solution. Penetrate heavy enemy defenses at night in full stealth mode, drop two (2!) bombs typically a GBU-10 Paveway II laser guided bomb. No radar, no air-to-air capability, no internal gun. But that one mission, it could do with aplomb as demonstrated during Desert Storm and the Panama Invasion of 1989 (yeah…that). It may be retired, but it appears the USAF continues to operate them for training and R&D uses.

Question: I saw the movie Blade Runner (1982) today and I didn't like it. Seeing as it seems to be regarded a classic, what did I miss?

Practical, not special, effects. Harrison Ford had just had his roles as Indiana Jones and Han Solo. Ridley Scott had just finished “Alien”; “Blade Runner” would be his 3rd film ever. Then, you have to watch it in a theater with a big (big!) screen and a terrific sound system turned up. Preferably a night viewing. Bonus if it’s raining cats & dogs like it was when I watched it. I promise you it came across as one of the most intelligent futuristic sci-fi programs and damn scary with the implications of the future it envisioned, which was dark, void of humanity, wholly capitalized, and barren of anything endearing. The visuals, the music, the plot….just stunning. And my god — Sean Young AND Daryl Hannah. M. Emmett Walsh AND Rutger Hauer. Has there ever been better casting? It was depressing, fantastic, sad, thrilling, and just WOW! I emerged from the theater (into the rain). I knew right then I had seen a classic.

Question: In the naval aviation community, which carries more prestige, TOPGUN or Blue Angels?

Question: When a fighter jet had a listed max range ceiling, what does that actually mean when the plane or pilot is near that max or possibly over it? Just not recommended or?
Answer: I flew the A-7E for much of my Navy career. The published Service Ceiling in 42,000 feet. Later in my career I did a lot of Post Maintenance Check Flights (PMCF) to verify the aircraft was operating properly following major maintenance, e.g. engine change, major structural inspection, etc. On those PMCFs I used to take the aircraft as high as possible. I was darn lucky if I could reach 42,000 feet. The engine just runs out of thrust at that altitude. There’s simply not enough air. You could indeed fly at 42,000 feet, and maybe you could actually climb a few hundred feet higher if you were lightly loaded. But for all practical reasons, that’s as high as you can go. (Note: I do realize that many of today’s aircraft have much higher (50K+) service ceilings, especially some of the latest bizjets.) Nothing dramatic happens at 42,000 feet. No changes to the airplane’s handling…the engine just runs out of thrust. Control responsiveness diminishes for the same reason. But it’s perfectly flyable. Recommended or not? Not really recommended. Not really necessary. It’s challenging to control the aircraft at that altitude; it just gets “squirrely”. About the only reason to go that high that I can think of is to clear a thunderstorm, but honestly…it’s easier to just steer around it. There’s no tactical reason I know of to get as “high as you can go”. And for the airplane I flew, it just wasn’t very useful. Nothing you can do at 42,000 feet that you can’t do at 41,000 or 40,000 feet…or even in the high 30’s. BTW, when you are flying cross country in the US, if you’re flying up in the high 30k’s, you’re pretty much alone. Not much traffic up there. Great visibility though. ;-)

Want to be military pilot, complete college with the best grades possible, complete a commissioning program with the best scores possible…then you improve your chances greatly of getting selected for flight school.

It’s often a “see and destroy” kind of mission requiring visual acquisition of the target. For example, there was a recent story of a US submarine, an Ohio class ballistic missile sub, that transited the Straits of San Juan de Fuca (the main access to the pacific from the Puget Sound area which is also home to the Bangor submarine base). The submarine was on the surface and was accompanied by four A-10s. Why this was done is unclear, but it epitomizes the non-CAS missions as “armed interdiction”. Question: Why is the U.S. spending 100 million on high tech wonders like the the F-35, complicated to operate, require pilots, and prone to crashes when it would be cheaper to push out basic air frames, in pilot less drone modes, to achieve air superiority?
Answer: No. Certainly not currently. First of all, your question is along the lines of “when did you stop beating your wife”. The F-35 is not prone to crashes. It has an envious safety record. But every mishap gets highlighted in the media like it’s a national emergency. If you fly high-performance aircraft a lot, you will at some point experience mishaps and accidents. So put that notion aside; not true. What makes the F-35 expensive is the incredible performance, stealth, engine, and sensor fusion. If you wanted an air superiority drone, you would still need all that. Then you’d have to somehow replace the sophisticated analog computer in the cockpit — vision, judgement, experience, instant learning. Air Superiority is a very challenging mission requiring all those attributes in spades. The pilot isn’t an unnecessary accessory, it’s the critical element in mission effectiveness. Drones are amazing and getting better all the time. They’re nearly ideal for certain missions, such as reconnaissance, forward observation, and as an asymmetrical force multiplier. But they have disadvantages: the most effective drones still need a man in the loop, that makes them vulnerable to jamming. They typically need GPS to be effective. Their efficacy in a degraded mode plummets to near zero. And they can’t apply judgement beyond what they’re programmed to do. Don’t get me wrong, for many missions they’re ideal, but Air Superiority isn’t one of them—at least yet.

Question: When the USN transitioned its A-7 squadrons to F-18s, how did they staff the squadrons? Did most A-7 pilots transition as well, or did they draw pilots from other sources? Did transitioning A-7 pilots have difficulty acclimating to the F-18?
Answer: I was in one of those A-7 squadrons. The F/A-18 replaced both the USN F-4s and A-7s. For the most part, the pilots in those squadrons transitioned to the F/A-18, and did so successfully. But it was a mix. And yes, some brand newly winged aviators were sent directly to F/A-18s. Every squadron needs a mix of senior, mid, and junior officers. And there were a number of exceptions. (I’ll use my A-7 squadron as an example.) If you had nearly completed your squadron tour, say having served 30 months out of a 36 month tour, then you would likely not make the transition with the squadron. Instead, you’d receive orders to your next assignment a few months earlier than normal. Also, we had a few Reserve pilots who were on active duty. They were not afforded an opportunity to transition to F/A-18s, only regular Navy. If you had just arrived in your A-7 squadron, maybe just a few months there, you were likely to be re-assigned to another A-7 squadron that had not yet been scheduled for transition. This happened to some of my shipmates who had been in the squadron < 6 months; they went to other A-7 squadrons (and their future fate depended on when that squadron transitioned.) And, regrettably, some squadrons were decommissioned. The plan to transition A-7s to F/A-18s was running well behind schedule in the mid-80s. And some squadrons that would normally have transitioned were instead decommissioned, as their transition date slipped further and further to the right. Take for example, a squadron that had just returned from a routine deployment. Normally, the carrier goes into a maintenance period while the Air Wing goes into a reduced flying schedule for at least a few months. If such a squadron was due to transition to the F/A-18, and their transition schedule was slipping, then possibly that squadron would be decommissioned. And then later — typically many months later, often over a year — a new squadron would be stood up. The re-assignment of pilots from the decommissioned squadrons fell into the categories above, although since the squadron was decommissioned due to schedule issues, assignment to an F/A-18 billet did not happen. Most went to other A-7 squadrons or to their next duty station. A lot of good-byes as the Navy said farewell to some long-standing squadrons. The decommissioning mostly affected the A-7 squadrons. My understanding was the remaining USN F-4 squadrons all transitioned pretty much on schedule.

Question: What is the reason for some fighter jets needing computer assistance to maintain stability on the ground and in flight?
Answer: That’s not an error; it’s a feature. And it’s highly desirable. Beginning with the YF-16 and YF-17, aircraft manufacturers have build aircraft that are inherently unstable. That is, without computer control over the flight regime, the aircraft would then tumble, roll, and pitch up/down. That’s good news. The more unstable an aircraft is, the more maneuverable and agile it is. Those two prototypes were first out of the gate, but today’s front line fighters (F-22, F-35, Gripen, Typhoon, those amazing Russian aircraft that they demo but never deploy, etc.) are all designed to be inherently unstable. That is what gives them the amazing aerodynamic qualities that provide superb agility, turning, twisting, all while maintaining control over the aircraft due to the computer-controlled fly-by-wire flight control system. And the fly-by-wire systems can do things that conventional flight control systems cannot do, such as split the horizontal stabilizers with one up and one down, to enhance roll performance. Stunning. Check out this F-22 doing…well doing something I never thought possible in a jet, that’s for sure. If you’re flying a large commercial airliner, such as a Boeing 777, then you want a very stable, not-easily pushed about airplane and control system. If you’re flying an F-35, you want exactly the opposite. That’s what makes it a superior fighter (among other things). Oh…no airplane requires computer control to maintain stability on the ground. Gravity provides that for free.

Question: How fast can modern fighter aircraft (F-16, F-18, etc.) go? How long does it take them to reach their top speed from a standing start?
Answer: Many of the modern fighter aircraft can fly in the “mid” mach+ range — 1.5 - 1.8 mach. (The F-15 has a somewhat faster top-end.) But that is not their normal speed; that’s the top-end speed. It would be like asking a driver how fast does his Mercedes can go. Yeah…it can reach maybe 150mph, but that is not how the car is driven. And 1.5 mach is not how the F-16, F-15, or F-35 is flown. Normally, jet fighters cruise at about 300–400 knots. Faster of course in certain scenarios. Slower in others. And from a standing start? You mean from takeoff? Well, first of all, the USN F/A-18 gets a head start because it leaves the aircraft carrier at about 140–150 knots, and that takes about 2 seconds. So it gets a good headstart on say the F-16, which has to roll down the runway for a bit before take off. LOL… In general, I would guess that today’s high-end fighter jets can reach their top speed in 4–5 minutes, even from a standing start. But let me emphasize — speed is not everything in a jet fighter, in fact the “top-end speed” is not really all that important. Acceleration is important, sustained “G” forces is important, energy decay rate is important, turn rate is important, agility is important — top-end speed; not so much. Fan boys love it, but speed is not what wins the fight. One of the huge improvement in today’s top-end fighter jets is the avionics, the sensor integration, fly-by-wire, and the systems management capabilities. What makes the F/A-18 so much better than the airplane I flew (A-7E) is the avionic systems are just amazing (radar, sensors, computer, displays, weapons management, etc.). Yes, the aerodynamic performance is dramatically increased, but the quantum lean in combat efficacy is the onboard systems.

Question: In a dogfight between two fighter jets, how would the outcome be determined if neither could fire at the other due to proximity issues?
Answer: If neither fighter could fire, it wouldn’t really be a dogfight. It would be a draw and each fighter would disengage. A “draw” if you will. But here’s the thing. A dogfight is in generally to be avoided at all cost. Dogfights are unpredictable, mistakes happen, dissimilar aircraft often prevent prediction of a foe’s move —- and most importantly, the “best” airplane does not always win. A true dogfight is a crap shoot. I’ve told the story before of how I once shot down an F-15 with my trusty A-7E. That shouldn’t be possible given the F-15’s performance advantage, but the Eagle pilot made a mistake, and I had a shot. The best airplane does not always win a dogfight. The preferred way to destroy enemy aircraft is: 1) On the ground, with attack aircraft or better yet cruise missiles. 2) BVR - shoot the bad guy with a long-range missile and kill him before the merge. 3) Aggressive surface-to-air (SAM) missiles. Yes, you can establish air superiority over the battlefield if you have an advanced SAM capability. Dogfights make good Hollywood movies, but that is not the preferred way to destroy enemy aircraft.

Question: Why can't the USAF also be sea-based and not just land-based? How come the USN/USMC are both sea based and land based?
Answer: It’s all about Roles & Missions. And having specific roles & missions allows for specialization. And believe me, inside the walls of the Pentagon those roles & missions are constantly reviewed, challenged, and altered. The budget fights are often quite ugly. Here are the various military missions as defined in US Title 10, the law that covers the military forces: Navy - The Navy shall be organized, trained, and equipped for the peacetime promotion of the national security interests and prosperity of the United States and for prompt and sustained combat incident to operations at sea. “prompt and sustained combat operations at sea” Army - The U.S. Army’s mission is to fight and win the nation’s wars by providing prompt, sustained land dominance across the full range of military operations and spectrum of conflict in support of combatant commanders. “land dominance” USMC - The Marine Corps shall be organized, trained, and equipped to provide fleet marine forces of combined arms, together with supporting air components, for service with the fleet in the seizure or defense of advanced naval bases and for the conduct of such land operations as may be essential to the prosecution of a naval campaign. “seizure of naval bases in support of prosecution of a naval campaign” USAF - It shall be organized, trained, and equipped primarily for prompt and sustained offensive and defensive air operations. “air operations” Okay..that’s the legal framework. But the point is that each service has specific roles & missions, and their training, equipment, and organization is designed to support those. The USAF is not responsible for combat at sea. Nor is it responsible for amphibious landings. The US Navy is not responsible for strategic bombers and missiles, except for the guided missile submarines, which really do not typically work in conjunction with other Naval forces. The US Navy does not operate tanks or other land-based combat equipment. The US Army does not provide air forces to conduct air-to-air operations. Nor does it maintain the ability to attack enemy ships. You could of course argue that there should be just a single “US Military”, but the separation of roles & missions has been shown to work quite well, and there’s no pressing need to fix something that isn’t broken AND take on 250 years of history and tradition.

Question: How long should it take a competent Ukrainian jet aircraft pilot to cross train on the F-16? What if they already speak and read some English? What about the ground maintenance crews?
Answer: TL; DR; 6–12 months An excellent question, and as a former USN Flight Instructor, I suspect the time frame is longer than we would like, or expect. I would say a minimum of 6 months, and possibly up to a year. The maintenance crews may take somewhat less, as those tasks are often quite specific in nature. Speaking English versus not speaking English might have limited impact for maintenance crews, more so for pilots. Let me reflect on something that happened when I was in USN flight training and early Fleet tours. During the advanced stage of my jet training, the Vietnam war finally ended, and the POWs returned home. Most of the Vietnam era POWs were pilots. And a great many of those guys wanted to resume their military aviation career, and they were fully accorded opportunities to do that. Many of the Naval Aviator former POWs were sent to the Training Command to re-train and re-fresh their flying skills. And I had a chance to fly with several. Now admittedly this is no where near the same thing as taking an experienced Ukrainian pilot who is current and physically fit, but still it’s an interesting case study. And there are some similarities and lessons to be learned, I believe. Some of the pilots had only been held as a POW for a few months; some for years. The whole re-train the POWs was a smorgashboard of skills, motivations, and experience. And of course, many of these former POWs had advanced in rank during their captivity; LTJGs were now LCDRs, CDRs were now CAPTs. Advancement in rank, but no concomitant advancement in aviation experience. Part of the issue was that the aircraft had changed. The A-4 had been replaced by the A-7. The F-8 had been replaced by the F-4. The A-1D Skyraider was gone completely. Even the training aircraft had changed from the TF-9J Cougar to the TA-4J Skyhawk. It went okay, but not great. The re-training took longer, and was less effective than envisioned. When the former POWs returned to the Fleet (where I flew with several), their aviation skills were behind their peers. Some LCDRs had as much difficulty flying on & off the boat as a brand new Ensign. Same with their tactical skills, which again had changed a lot following Vietnam. Again — not equivalent, but I think still relevant. So — lesson learned. Re-training even “experienced” pilots on a new, advanced aircraft can be fraught with risk, and will likely take longer than anticipated.

Question: For aspiring Naval Aviator who are also doing civilian pilot training before going to Naval OCS and Naval Flight School, what Pilot Ratings should one obtain before going to Naval OCS and Flight School that would help with getting a contract?
Answer: As a former flight instructor in the US Navy for two tours, I can say definitively that it does not matter one whit what civilian pilot ratings you have when you enter Navy Flight School. Nada. Zero. Zip. Zilch. Now, if you want to obtain various civilian pilot ratings before you start training, that’s perfectly fine of course, and it may give you somewhat of a head start on some of your other classmates. But military flight training is considerably different than civilian training. The Navy (and the USAF, USMC, and USCG) will teach you all you need to know about how to fly various military aircraft. Here’s an example: In civilian flight training, the student typically solos with about 10 hrs of flight time. I soloed in Navy flight school with 4 hrs of flight time, and that was not unusual. I flew my first jet at 24.5 hours. At 200 hrs, I had landed on an aircraft carrier about 10 times, flown 2 and 4 plane formations, full acrobatics, training in low level, high speed flight. Conducted aerial gunnery, ACM, strafing, and bombing. Oh…and fully qualified to fly in total IFR right down to 200–1/2, and had done so on several occasions. 200 hrs. The training is so much more intense, the ground school so much more challenging, and your entire life revolves around learning to fly. There’s simply nothing else like it. BTW, there is an FAA Military Competency Exam which after Navy flight training will easily qualify you for a commercial, instrument rating. I’ve seen it happen many times. Newly minted officers show up with a few hundred hours of flight time. Some with Commercial licenses. Some with some jet time, typically corporate. It just doesn’t matter. And in some cases, those with prior flight time have actually learned some techniques that are 1) not great flying techniques, and 2) actually detrimental to how the Navy teaches you to fly. So many examples I’ve seen. Do your best in OCS. Hopefully you’ll get assigned to flight training. Do your best in ground school and in the cockpit. It’s a magnificent experience and invaluable training. Just don’t think that civilian flight training and certifications will make a big difference. Fly Navy Jets.

Question: Is arresting gear cables on aircraft carriers modular or retractable? If I want to use a landing runway for take off, can I retract the cables?
Answer: The arresting gear cables on an aircraft carrier are retractable. There are four of them in the designated landing zone. The cables are retracted, put in “tension” for an arrested landing, and then are caught by the tailhook of the landing aircraft, and reel-out while dissipating the aircraft’s energy and bringing the aircraft to a full stop. Then the entire cycle starts all over again to wait for the next aircraft. When flight ops are not in progress, the cables just remain lying on the deck, and airplanes and other flight deck equipment can easily just drive over them. Aircraft launch from conventional carriers (what are called CATOBAR carriers) by using steam or electically powered catapults. The catapults are arranged such that they are clear of all the arresting cables; there’s no interference. If the aircraft carrier wants to, it can arrange to be landing and launching simultaneously.

And there is no question that the F-35 is a superior airplane in most areas…not all areas, but most. So there’s that. However, the F-35 costs quite a bit more to operate than the F-15EX. And for about 80% of the missions of a modern military air force, the F-15EX is more than adequate — impressive in fact. Add to that the problem that the F-35 is behind in production. If you order an F-35 today, it will likely not be delivered for several years. Whereas the F-15EX production line is pumping out aircraft quite quickly. You can probably buy one today and get it next year. And if you already operate F-15s, the savings in utilizing the investment already made in training, maintenance, and logistics would be a significant purchase factor. Many defense pundits have seen the F-15EX as a threat to the F-35 production numbers as they view the USAF budget as a zero-sum game; for every F-15EX the USAF purchases, that’s one less F-35 they’ll need for at least the next 15 years or so. But without question, the F-35 is proving to be a terrific aircraft. The sensor integration is absolutely amazing and if you ask any pilot which airplane he wants to take into combat, it would certainly be the Fat Amy F-35. There’s no question — it’s the best jet fighter in the world today. So…I think both the USAF and several allied nations will see the F-15EX as a prudent investment to meet near-term needs. And for non-US countries already operating the F-15 (Japan, Israel, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, SIngapore, South Korea), they will be sorely tempted to look at the F-15EX until perhaps a much upgraded F-35 becomes available (F-35 block upgrades and engine enhancement are already in the pipeline. Question: Can French fighter jets do midair refueling from American tanker aircraft, and vice versa?
Answer: Yes they can. Most USAF tanker aircraft have the capability to provide refueling either via the probe-drogue method, or via the boom method. All USAF aircraft, including fighter jets, use the boom method. It provides a higher flow rate for refueling. However, aircraft in the USN, USMC, and may allied nations use the probe-drogue method. So USAF tanker aircraft also provide that method of refueling, often via a refueling store on the outer wing station, such that they can maintain both the probe-drogue and boom methods. On dedicated tanker missions for the USN, USMC, or other allied nations, a USAF tanker will configure a “drogue” onto the base of the boom, and provide refueling that way. Since Desert Storm in the late 90s, the emphasis on joint warfare planning and operations has increased enormously. (A hard lesson learned from Desert Storm). So today, the alternate refueling methods are much more widely available than in the past. As we used to say when I flew the A-7E for the US Navy. All you had to do to convert to the USAF A-7D was change the sex. ;-)

There are sometimes where there is a cooperative agreement between the manufacturer and the US Government where an item is purchased, but the manufacturer owns the patent or intellectual property. Drug development is one such area. This approach can be used to reduce the cost of the initial purchase (as the IP is quite valuable), but does not give the Government full control over the production and sale of the product. For items relating to national defense, that’s typically not acceptable.

Question: Is there a US Navy aircraft that is similar to the Air Force's A-10 Warthog in function?
Answer: Not today. No…not really. And for good reason. The A-10 is a unique airplane designed almost exclusively for one mission: close air support (CAS) for the US Army. It was designed way back in 1970s, and entered service in 1977. About 700 were built. The primary threat in that timeframe was the large ground forces of the Warsaw Pact/Soviet Union. The WWIII US Army and USAF battlefront was envisioned as being in Central Europe, specifically the Fulda Gap in central Germany. That was when there was a West and East Germany; when most of Eastern Europe was still under Soviet control. And for that role, requiring the ‘servicing’ of an immense number of Soviet tanks, the A-10 was precisely the right solution. However, defense of central Europe is not a role or mission that the US Navy is responsible for. The Navy’s mission is for “prompt sustained combat operations at sea. In fact, in the 1980–1990s, the US Navy struggled with how it might contribute to winning the “war in central Europe”, but that’s a topic for another time. But things change, and in 1989/1990 the Soviet Union collapsed almost overnight, and with that, much of the need for the A-10 and its tank-killing 30mm gun. Gone was the primary raison d'être for the Warthog. And about the same time, very precise weapons were being developed that relied on laser guidance and GPS. These developments provided the precision of CAS with more survivable stand-off distances. So while the A-10 is still around, albeit in limited numbers, today neither the USN nor the USMC maintain dedicated CAS aircraft, relying instead on other multi-mission aircraft to perform that role with precision-guided weapons: aircraft such as the F/A-18, AV-8B, and now the F-35. In addition to CAS, those aircraft are also capable of many other missions (air-to-air, deep strike, war-at-sea, etc.) that are not well matched to the A-10 The USAF has taken a similar position, mostly relying on the F-16 for the CAS mission in addition to the smaller number of A-10s in operation.

Name: David Tussey
Question: Is Marine Corps aviation also considered as 'naval aviation'? Or just being 'marine aviation' in its own right?
Answer: Sort of. Yes. Both. The US Navy Aviation Training Command trains all the aviators for the USMC, the USN, and the US Coast Guard. And those pilots all wear the same Wings of Gold. USMC jet pilots carrier qualify just like their USN counterparts. And USMC jet fighter squadrons routinely deploy aboard Navy aircraft carriers. Typically one squadron every year or so. The training command instructor pilots (IP) come from both the USN and the USMC. I was an IP in one of the Texas-based jet training squadron, and about 1/3 of the IPs were Marines. That builds a lot of camaraderie and mutual respect right from the get-go. The Department of the Navy procures all the aircraft for the US Navy and US Marine Corps. For the most part, the services fly the same airplanes, although there are specialties, such as the MV-22 and F-35B STOVL model for the USMC, and the same for a few models for the USN such as the F/A-18 Super Hornet, while the USMC operated the legacy Hornet. The Blue Angels flight demonstration team has both USN and USMC pilots. The USMC operates the “Marine One” helicopters that fly the President, Vice-President, and other senior government officials. The USN operates VIP aircraft out of Andrews AFB for some of the official government trips with senior officials. The USMC operates similar VIP aircraft out of Fort Worth, TX. The missions, the aircraft, and the training are very, very similar for both Services. And that cooperation between USN and USMC aviation communities has been going on (successfully) for many years, and there’s no indication it will change.

Question: Is there really a 6th generation fighter on aircraft carriers or just a pipe dream?

That’s how the B-2, F-117, B-21, and F-22 programs were developed. At some point the program may “come into the light”, but we’re not there yet. Meanwhile, let your imagination run wild.
